purpose: This medicine is used to help reduce the number of painful episodes called vaso-occlusive crises (VOCs) in people who have sickle cell disease and are 16 years of age or older. These painful crises happen when sickle-shaped blood cells block blood flow in your vessels. By using this medication, you may have fewer of these painful episodes each year.
how_it_works: Sickle cell disease causes your red blood cells to become stiff and crescent-shaped, which makes them stick together and block your blood vessels, causing pain. This medicine works by blocking a protein called P-selectin, which acts like a sticky glue that helps those abnormal cells clump together and stick to blood vessel walls. By blocking that sticky protein, this medication helps keep your blood flowing more smoothly and reduces the chance of a painful blockage.
common_side_effects: Nausea, joint pain, back pain, fever, and reactions during or shortly after the IV infusion such as chills, tiredness, shortness of breath, sweating, or skin redness. Most infusion reactions are mild to moderate.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have any signs of an infusion reaction during or within 24 hours of your treatment, such as fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, or difficulty breathing. There is also a potential increased risk of bleeding, so tell your doctor about all other medications you take, especially blood thinners. This medicine has not been well studied during pregnancy or breastfeeding, so talk to your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
typical_dosing: This medication is given as an IV infusion (through a vein) by a healthcare provider. The usual dose is 5 mg per kilogram of your body weight. You will receive it once at the start, then again 2 weeks later, and then once every 4 weeks after that. Each infusion takes about 30 minutes.
